clinicalPearls: Steatotic liver disease (SLD) is the most common cause of chronic liver disease in the US and worldwide; metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) and steatohepatitis (MASH) now replace the older terms NAFLD and NASH, with ~98% population overlap (Harrison 22e p.2700-2701).

Diagnosis of MASLD requires hepatic steatosis plus little/no alcohol intake (<20 g/d women, <30 g/d men) and at least one cardiometabolic risk factor (overweight/obesity, hypertension, dyslipidemia, insulin resistance/T2DM) (Harrison 22e p.2700, 2703).
Most patients are asymptomatic; MASLD is typically detected incidentally via raised ALT or steatosis on imaging done for other reasons (Harrison 22e p.2702-2703).

Disease spans a dynamic, potentially reversible spectrum: simple steatosis (MASL) -> steatohepatitis (MASH) -> fibrosis -> cirrhosis/HCC; chronic steatohepatitis is the primary driver of fibrosis, and fibrosis severity is the chief predictor of liver-related morbidity/mortality (Harrison 22e p.2700-2701, 2704).

FIB-4 (age, AST, ALT, platelets) is the recommended first-line noninvasive score with excellent negative predictive value: FIB-4 <1.3 = low risk (manage in primary care), >=2.67 = moderate/high risk warranting a secondary test (elastography or ELF) (Harrison 22e p.2704-2705).

T2DM is the strongest risk factor for MASLD acquisition, fibrosis progression, and HCC; the MASLD-T2DM relationship is bidirectional, so patients with MASLD should be screened for T2DM (Harrison 22e p.2703).

Foundational treatment is lifestyle modification with weight loss: ~5% weight loss improves steatosis, while >10% improves MASH and can reverse fibrosis; cardiovascular risk reduction and treatment of metabolic comorbidities apply to all patients (Harrison 22e p.2706).
Statins are safe across the MASLD spectrum and indicated for dyslipidemia given high cardiovascular risk; reluctance to use them is not supported by evidence of liver harm (Harrison 22e p.2707).
harrison.pathophysiology: MASLD arises from imbalance between energy intake and expenditure: excess caloric intake, reduced physical activity, and limited peripheral adipose expansion drive visceral adiposity, insulin resistance, and metabolic dysfunction. Hepatocyte triglyceride accumulates from increased free fatty acid delivery (dietary uptake, adipose lipolysis, de novo lipogenesis), impaired fatty acid disposal, or impaired triglyceride export; triglyceride storage itself is relatively safe, so steatosis per se does not damage the liver but is a biomarker of metabolic dysfunction. When adaptive mechanisms are overwhelmed, lipotoxicity from dysfunctional lipid handling injures and kills hepatocytes, producing steatohepatitis (MASH) with inflammation and ballooned hepatocytes. Repeated/protracted MASH triggers regenerative responses that become maladaptive, promoting progressive fibrosis (replacement of functional parenchyma by scar) and primary liver cancer; cirrhosis represents futile repair. Heritable factors (e.g., PNPLA3, TM6SF2, MBOAT7 variants), epigenetic influences, gut microbiota alterations, and environmental factors (high-fat/high-sugar diets) modify susceptibility (Harrison 22e p.2701-2702).
additionalDifferentials: Alcohol-associated liver disease (ALD) and the intermediate MetALD category (metabolic dysfunction with social alcohol use, 20-50 g/d women, 30-60 g/d men)

Inborn errors of metabolism (abetalipoproteinemia, cholesterol ester storage disease, galactosemia, glycogen storage disease, hereditary fructose intolerance, homocystinuria, systemic carnitine deficiency, tyrosinemia)

harrison.prognosis: Variable and stage-dependent. The 10-year probability of liver-related morbidity/mortality is negligible with steatosis alone, so this group is managed conservatively. Fibrosis severity is the primary predictor of outcome: average fibrosis progression is roughly one stage every 14 years in steatosis versus one stage every 7 years in MASH; once at stage >=F2 ('at-risk MASH') the risk of further progression and bad outcomes rises. Once MASLD-related cirrhosis develops, progression to decompensation runs 3-20% per year and annual primary liver cancer incidence can reach 1-2% per year, prompting biannual HCC surveillance and variceal screening. Cirrhosis can regress, and MASLD outcomes after liver transplantation are generally good in well-selected patients, though comorbid diabetes, obesity, and CVD limit candidacy and disease may recur post-transplant. MASLD is also a premalignant condition increasing risk of primary and extrahepatic malignancy even in noncirrhotic livers (Harrison 22e p.2701, 2704, 2708).
pitfalls: Failing to exclude significant alcohol intake and other chronic liver diseases (viral, autoimmune, iron/copper overload, alpha-1 antitrypsin) before attributing steatosis to MASLD.
Assuming normal liver enzymes exclude MASLD - they do not; normal ALT 'reference ranges' are inflated by including people with undiagnosed liver disease.
Relying on liver tests for staging - aminotransferases, alkaline phosphatase, bilirubin, albumin, and PT may all be completely normal even with significant disease.
MASLD can occur in lean individuals (BMI <25, or <23 in Asians), especially with truncal/visceral adiposity, so a normal BMI does not exclude it.
FIB-4 has reduced accuracy in patients >65 and <35 years and is a less robust predictor in T2DM, so a secondary noninvasive test is needed in these groups.
Liver biopsy is limited by sampling error, inter/intraobserver variability (worse with cores <2 cm), and gives only a static snapshot of disease activity.
harrison.severityClassification: Histopathologic/fibrosis staging spectrum: simple steatosis (MASL) -> steatohepatitis (MASH) -> fibrosis -> cirrhosis. Fibrosis stages F0 (none), F1 (minimal), F2 (significant), F3 (advanced/bridging), F4 (cirrhosis, further stratified into compensated and decompensated). 'At-risk MASH' = MASH with fibrosis stage >=F2. Noninvasive risk stratification: FIB-4 <1.3 low risk, >=1.3 intermediate, >=2.67 moderate/high; secondary tests VCTE <8 kPa low / 8-12 intermediate / >12 high, ELF <7.7 low / 7.7-9.8 intermediate / >9.8 high (Harrison 22e p.2704-2705).
management: Institute lifestyle intervention as the cornerstone, with sustained weight loss through calorie restriction and increased physical activity to reverse the underlying metabolic dysfunction

Optimise cardiometabolic drivers by controlling type 2 diabetes, dyslipidaemia and hypertension, and treating obesity with GLP-1 receptor agonists and, in eligible patients, metabolic (bariatric) surgery

Consider disease-specific pharmacotherapy for confirmed steatohepatitis with fibrosis, notably the thyroid-hormone-receptor-beta agonist resmetirom, with GLP-1 agonists, pioglitazone or vitamin E as options in selected patients
Advise alcohol minimisation and provide hepatitis immunisation to limit additional liver injury
Risk-stratify and monitor fibrosis with FIB-4 and elastography, referring higher-risk patients from primary care to hepatology
Surveil for complications of advanced fibrosis and cirrhosis, including hepatocellular carcinoma screening and variceal surveillance, and screen for coexisting type 2 diabetes
Prioritise cardiovascular risk reduction as the leading cause of death, and refer for liver transplantation assessment in decompensated cirrhosis
